summary: This standards-track document extends how OSPFv3 Link State Advertisements are formatted, going beyond the fixed format of RFC 5340. Without it, attributes of links and IPv6 prefixes have to be advertised in separate LSAs and matched up. The extension makes OSPFv3 easier to extend.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8362 defines a TLV-based form of OSPFv3 link-state advertisements. It carries existing routing information in the new format and leaves room for additional attributes, with rules for compatibility and migration.

questions: what is the ospfv3 extended lsa format
how to migrate ospfv3 to extended lsas
subtitle: A TLV-based format for extending OSPFv3 link-state advertisements while preserving existing routing semantics.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3's fixed-format LSAs require extra attributes for links and prefixes to be advertised separately and correlated with the original LSAs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Extended LSAs that encode existing information in TLVs and allow optional TLVs and sub-TLVs to add information.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 gains an extensible LSA format and defined migration modes. The RFC updates RFC 5340 and RFC 5838.

today: RFC 8362 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2018. It updates RFC 5340 and RFC 5838; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 LSAs Need an Extension
sections.content:
OSPFv3's fixed-format Link State Advertisements (LSAs), defined by RFC 5340, are difficult to extend. Without an extension, attributes associated with links and advertised IPv6 prefixes must be carried in separate LSAs and correlated with the fixed-format LSAs.

RFC 8362 moves the existing information into Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples and permits additional TLVs to carry new information. It provides TLV-based encodings for base OSPFv3 and address-family support, and updates RFC 5838. The RFC aims to preserve the existing LSA semantics and most encoding details.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixed-format LSAs have limited room for new information. Extended LSAs use TLVs to carry the existing information and allow more attributes to be added.

sections.title: Extended LSA Types
sections.content:
Each Extended LSA gets a new function code based on its Legacy LSA counterpart: the function code is increased by 32, or 0x20. This uses less of the function-code space than assigning a format bit. The U-bit MUST be set so routers that do not understand an Extended LSA still flood it.

The RFC defines Extended forms of the Router, Network, Inter-Area-Prefix, Inter-Area-Router, AS-External, Type-7, Link, and Intra-Area-Prefix LSAs. Function code 38 is unused and MUST NOT be allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Legacy LSA has an Extended counterpart with a function code 32 higher. The U-bit tells routers that do not understand the new format to continue flooding it.

sections.title: TLVs and Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Extended LSA bodies contain one or more nested TLV tuples. Each TLV begins with a 16-bit Type and 16-bit Length, followed by its value. Length counts only the value in octets. TLVs and nested sub-TLVs are padded to 4-octet alignment, and padding is excluded from Length.

TLVs and sub-TLVs MAY appear in any order. A specification for each TLV defines whether it is required and how repeated instances are handled. The RFC defines eight top-level TLV types for router links, attached routers, inter-area prefixes and routers, external and intra-area prefixes, and link-local addresses. It also defines forwarding-address and route-tag sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TLV has a type, a value length, and a value. Four-octet alignment padding is added between entries, but the length does not count that padding.

sections.title: Link, Prefix, and Forwarding Information
sections.content:
The Router-Link TLV describes one router link and is used in an E-Router-LSA. The Attached-Routers TLV lists routers attached to a multi-access network and is used in an E-Network-LSA. Other top-level TLVs represent inter-area prefixes, reachable inter-area routers, external prefixes, intra-area prefixes, and IPv4 or IPv6 link-local addresses. A TLV in an Extended LSA where it is not applicable MUST be ignored.

The External-Prefix TLV can contain IPv4 or IPv6 forwarding-address sub-TLVs and a Route-Tag sub-TLV. Only the first instance of each is used; later instances MUST be ignored. The RFC adds a prefix N-bit with value 0x20, which can mark a host address identifying the advertising router. The bit is a hint for choosing a preferred address to reach that router.

Some Extended LSAs must contain exactly one matching TLV to preserve existing semantics and incremental SPF computation. E-Router-LSAs and E-Link-LSAs can contain multiple applicable link or prefix TLVs as specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TLV describes one kind of routing information and is valid only in specified Extended LSA types. Some LSAs require one matching TLV; others can carry multiple link or prefix entries.

sections.title: Malformed LSAs and Unknown Extensions
sections.content:
An Extended LSA with inconsistent length or encoding errors MUST NOT be installed in the Link State Database, acknowledged, or flooded. An LSA is malformed if required TLVs are missing or if a TLV length exceeds its container or is below the minimum for that TLV. Receivers SHOULD count or log malformed LSAs for an administrator.

Unrecognized TLVs and sub-TLVs are ignored. A specification introducing a new TLV MUST say whether partial deployment is supported and how to prevent or handle it. Future TLVs and sub-TLVs MUST be optional, although a TLV can require its own sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers discard malformed Extended LSAs rather than storing or forwarding them. They ignore TLVs they do not recognize, and future extensions must explain their partial-deployment behavior.

sections.title: Migrating from Legacy LSAs
sections.content:
In full migration, enabling ExtendedLSASupport causes a router to originate Extended LSAs and use them for SPF computation. Areas can be migrated separately using AreaExtendedLSASupport; Legacy AS-External-LSAs continue to be originated and used for their computation.

A routing domain or area can migrate without disruption by running separate OSPFv3 instances. The instance using Extended LSAs initially has lower preference. Once the routing information bases are checked, operators can prefer the Extended-LSA instance and later remove the Legacy instance. In sparse mode, routers continue using Legacy LSAs for SPF and originate Extended LSAs only for additional functionality, with only the TLVs that function requires.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can migrate an area to Extended LSAs in stages. Sparse mode keeps Legacy LSAs for routing calculations and adds Extended LSAs only when a new function needs them.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA adds nine Extended LSA types to the OSPFv3 LSA Function Codes registry and assigns 0x20 to the N-bit in the Prefix-Options registry. The RFC creates registries for Extended LSA TLVs and sub-TLVs. Their code points are shared across Extended LSAs; each definition states where a TLV applies.

For top-level TLVs, values 9 through 32767 use IETF Review or IESG Approval; 32768 through 33023 are for experimental use; 33024 through 45055 are First Come First Served; and 45056 through 65535 are not assigned at this time. The sub-TLV registry uses the same later ranges, starting its IETF Review range at 4.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA maintains shared registries for the new TLVs and sub-TLVs. The RFC defines which values need IETF review, which are experimental, and which ranges are held back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Extended LSAs have the same security concerns as OSPFv3 in RFC 5340. Implementations must also ensure that malformed TLV or sub-TLV combinations do not cause serious OSPFv3 failures.

The RFC notes that a TLV-based format would simplify an extension if digital signing of OSPFv3 LSAs were required in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing OSPFv3 security considerations still apply. Implementations must reject malformed extensions safely rather than fail during processing.
